n: Seeing that Amulek has silenced Zeezrom and that Zeezrom is trembling with guilt, Alma steps in to confirm Amulek’s words and explain the scriptures more deeply.

f.w: to establish the words of Amulek
f.g: Alma acts as the second witness, reinforcing Amulek’s testimony.

n: A large crowd hears what Alma says to Zeezrom.
Alma tells Zeezrom he has been caught lying — not only to men but to God, who knows his every thought and has revealed them to Alma and Amulek.
Alma lays out Zeezrom’s plan: to deceive the people and turn them against the missionaries — a scheme as subtle as the devil himself.
Zeezrom was acting as the adversary’s tool. And Alma’s warning applies to everyone listening, not only to Zeezrom.
This was Satan’s trap to bind the people in chains and drag them to destruction.
Zeezrom trembles even more, convinced of God’s power and that Alma and Amulek truly knew his heart by the spirit of prophecy.

f.w: the thoughts and intents of his heart

n: Zeezrom now begins sincerely asking questions. What did Amulek mean about everyone rising from the dead to be judged?

f.g: A turning point — the accuser becomes a seeker.

n: Alma explains a key principle: many are given to know God’s mysteries, but they may only share what God allows, according to people’s readiness and diligence.
Those who harden their hearts receive less; those who don’t receive more and more, until they know God’s mysteries in full. Revelation grows with openness.

f.w: the greater portion of the word

n: Those who keep hardening their hearts lose even what they had, until the devil leads them captive. That loss of light is what “the chains of hell” means.
Alma returns to Amulek’s teaching about death, resurrection, and judgment by works.
If we have hardened our hearts so that God’s word is not in us, we will be condemned.

f.g: Dreadful; full of awe and fear.

n: Our words, works, and thoughts will all condemn us. Ashamed, we would wish the mountains would fall on us to hide us from God.

f.w: our thoughts will also condemn us
the rocks and the mountains to fall upon us

n: But no one can hide. All will stand before God and admit his judgments are just — and that he is merciful and able to save all who believe and repent.
Alma introduces the “second death” — spiritual death. Those who die in their sins also die as to righteousness, cut off from God.
Their torment is like a lake of fire and brimstone that never ends — chained down under Satan’s power.

f.w: a lake of fire and brimstone
f.g: Brimstone = burning sulfur; a vivid image of remorse and anguish.

n: For them it is as if no redemption were made; justice cannot redeem the unrepentant, and since resurrected bodies cannot die, there is no escape.

f.w: as though there had been no redemption made

n: The people grow even more astonished.

f.g: Alma’s teachings deeply affect the crowd.

n: Antionah, a chief ruler, challenges Alma: how can a person rise from death and become immortal, with a soul that never dies?

f.g: A leading official in Ammonihah; he raises a scriptural objection.

n: He cites Genesis: God placed cherubim and a flaming sword to keep Adam and Eve from the tree of life. Doesn’t that prove humans cannot live forever?
Alma welcomes the question — it is just what he was about to explain. Adam’s fall made all mankind lost and fallen.
If Adam had eaten from the tree of life right then, he would never have died, and God’s word — “thou shalt surely die” — would have failed.

f.w: If thou eat thou shalt surely die

n: Death came, but God gave a span of time to repent. This life is a probation — a time to prepare to meet God.

f.w: a time to prepare to meet God

n: Without the plan of redemption, prepared from the foundation of the world, there would be no resurrection. But there is such a plan.

f.g: Alma’s preferred name for God’s plan of salvation.

n: Had Adam and Eve eaten from the tree of life, they would have lived forever in their sins with no time to prepare — forever miserable. The cherubim were an act of mercy.
Instead, people must die and then face judgment.

f.w: appointed unto men that they must die

n: God saw it was wise that people should understand what he had set in place for them.
So God sent angels to teach mankind and show them his glory.

f.w: he sent angels to converse with them

n: From then on people called on God’s name, and God revealed the plan of redemption according to their faith, repentance, and holy works.
After the first transgression, humans became “as gods, knowing good from evil,” free to act by their own will. So God gave new commandments.

f.w: as gods, knowing good from evil

n: God first taught them the plan, then gave commandments. Breaking them brings the second death, because justice cannot simply be erased.

f.w: the works of justice could not be destroyed

n: But God called to them in the name of his Son: repent, harden not your hearts, and I will have mercy through my Only Begotten Son.

f.w: in the name of his Son

n: Whoever repents has a claim on mercy through Christ and will enter God’s rest.

f.g: The peace and glory of God’s presence.

n: Whoever hardens his heart will not enter God’s rest.
Alma applies it to his listeners. Hardening their hearts provokes God as Israel did in the wilderness — “the provocation” — bringing the last death as well as the first.

f.g: Israel’s rebellion in the wilderness, when they were barred from the promised land.

n: Alma includes himself: since we know these things are true, let us repent and enter into God’s rest.

f.g: Alma speaks as one of them, not above them.
